terms.comment: Pliny’s term for the year with the added day. Caesar fixed the year at 365 days, adding a day every fourth year (Suet. Jul. 40.1). The Romans did not add a 29 February: they counted the sixth day before the Kalends of March twice, whence late Latin bisextus, the leap day.

evidence: Plin. NH 2.35: ūnus intercalārius diēs additur
Traupman 78–79: ante diem bis VI Kalendās Mārtiās

terms.comment: The medieval and Church term, from bisextus, the leap day (Censorinus, Ammianus; Lewis & Short, who call the spelling bissextus an error).

phrases.latin: ūnus diēs quārtō quōque annō intercalārētur
phrases.english: (Caesar arranged that) one day should be added every fourth year

phrases.latin: quam ob causam quīntō annō ūnus intercalārius diēs additur
phrases.english: for this reason an extra day is added every fourth year (“in the fifth year”, counting both ends)
